catalog_quote: Vowels may be long or short. Contrast between long and short vowels occurs only in the final and the penultimate syllable of the word: káun [kā́ʔun] ‘eat’ and nagdá [nagdā́] ‘is bringing’. Further, there is only one long vowel per word. There is also a phoneme of stress which has a very low contrastive function. For the most part stress can be determined by the phonological make-up of the word: 1 stress falls on the long vowel of the word if the word has a long vowel: nagdá [nagdā́], káun [kā́ʔun]. 2 for words that have no long vowel, stress is on the penultimate if it is closed: tan-aw [tánʔaw] ‘see’; mugbù [múgbuʔ] ‘short’. If the penultimate is open and short, stress is on the ultimate: mala [malá] ‘dry’. Occasionally, in words with a closed penult the final syllable is stressed (marked here with a wedge): mandǎr [mandár] ‘order’; dughǐt [dughít] ‘instrument for poking’. In words wit…
sweep_summary: Cebuano (cebu1242) is in the catalog as weight-hedged on Wolff 1972 sec. 3.0 (verified verbatim this search of works with stress in the title in the held Gutenberg e-text). this search of works with stress in the title's single title hit, Shryock 1993 'A metrical analysis of stress in Cebuano' (Lingua 91:103-148), is squarely about word stress in this language and is the field's only dedicated analysis, but remains unreadable: Semantic Scholar CLOSED, Unpaywall closed with no repository copy, OpenAlex no record, Elsevier abstract API returns no abstract, ScienceDirect serves only a bot-check page, archive.org/eScholarship/fatcat yield nothing; it is online with a university library login - priority high for a first-hand read of pp. 104-112 (weight rule, secondary stress, exception class). Its content reaches us second-hand and consistently: the StressTyp2 entry(heavy CVC/CVV penult stressed unless ultima is CVV(C); light-light -> final; secondary stress on alternate syllables leftward) and Xu 2020 (held, read this search of works with stress in the title), whose instrumental re-elicitation of Shryock's word list finds that a closed penult always takes primary stress (Spanish loans excepted) and an open penult takes stress only when long, otherwise final. Zorc 1977 p. 50 (held) agrees for all Bisayan dialects. Two open citing works were downloaded (McGarrity 2003 Rutgers diss; Paramore 2025 Phonology): neither states Cebuano stress placement. Huneety et al. 2020 (Cebuano learners of Arabic, IJAL) is an L2 study; DOAJ abstract only, site behind an automated-access block. Nothing found contradicts the catalog's weight-hedged coding; the best first-hand statement read this search of works with stress in the title is Xu 2020 sec. 4.1, which confirms but does not supersede Wolff 1972.

new_statements.quote: In summary, when the penult is closed, it always receives primary stress, as seen in (3)-(4), with the exceptions being words that either are loanwords or have loanwords as the base. However, when the penult is open, the primary stress may fall on the final syllable, the penult, or even the antepenult. This does not seem to depend on the weight of the final syllable, which most likely receives the stress if it does not fall on the penult, as shown in (5)-(8). ... Antepenultimate stress is only observed in two situations: either the word is a Spanish loan and the syllable that is stressed in the Spanish counterpart retains the stress, or the word is formed by partial reduplication, as in (9).

new_statements.reading: First-hand elicitation (one speaker, instrumentally checked: duration and F1/F2 are the cues) of Shryock's word list: a closed penult always takes primary stress (Spanish loans excepted); with an open penult stress is penult when the penult vowel is long (analyzed by Shryock and Wolff as long, set (5)) and final when it is short (set (6)); antepenult only in loans and CV-reduplicated agentives. This is the same long-vowel > closed-penult > final-default hierarchy as Wolff 1972 sec. 3.0, with the same loan exception class; it confirms the 'weight-hedged' coding and adds that the final syllable's closure does not matter. Zorc 1977 p. 50 (held; re-extracted page) independently states for all Bisayan dialects incl. Cebuano: 'The vowel in an accented open penult (CV) is long.. In all dialects studied (except Kuy) stems or derivatives with a closed penult [CVC.CV(C)] are accented on the penult (see 10.2.1.)'.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the held Wolff 1972 Gutenberg e-text at Introduction sec. 3.0 (lines 484-501), and the 3.21 transcription note at lines 529-538, exactly as the locator says; the stage-V second reader had already re-derived 18/20 example agreements with the two mismatches being Wolff's own wedge-marked exception class. (2) Deciding source: a 1972 dictionary introduction, but by the field's principal Cebuano describer and first-hand; the classification 'weight-hedged' (long vowel > closed penult > final default, with 'for the most part'/'occasionally' hedges and a declared loan exception class) is corroborated by three independent lines we now hold or have seen: Xu 2020 (held; instrumental study re-eliciting Shryock's list: closed penult -> penult 'regardless of the structure of other syllables', exceptions are Spanish loans), StressTyp2's carry of Shryock

sources.note: The only dedicated (46 pp.) analysis of Cebuano primary and secondary stress; our record carries it second-hand via the StressTyp2 entryand Xu 2020's re-elicitation. Reading pp. 104-112 directly would let the the secondary-stress rule (secondary stress) and the exception class (antepenult stress, loan -ar/-ir finals) be quoted first-hand and could lift the weight-sensitive (tentative) reading to a firm weight statement.
